title: 10 Ways To Make Time-Out More Effective
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a classroom management plan does not need to be complicated to work; what matters most is how consistently and skillfully a teacher carries out its consequences, and time-out is his central example. He offers ten specific practices for making time-out effective: modeling the procedure in detail, never wavering on enforcement, briefly telling students why they are being separated, avoiding lectures during or on the way to time-out, giving students nothing to do during a recess time-out, personally supervising the consequence, having the class ignore students who are in time-out, letting students decide when they are ready to return (for in-class time-out), not holding grudges once the time-out ends, and making the classroom fun enough that students genuinely feel they are missing out. Throughout, he stresses that the power of any consequence lies not in the plan itself but in the manner of its delivery. The piece is written as a practical checklist for teachers who already use time-out but want to sharpen its impact.
points: Effectiveness lies in 'the how' of enforcing a consequence, not in the complexity of the classroom management plan itself.
Consistency is critical: teachers should never waver on sending a student to time-out once a rule is broken, regardless of what else is happening.
Lecturing before, during, or after time-out undermines the consequence and breeds resentment; the time-out itself should be the only consequence.
Personally supervising time-out, especially during recess, signals to students that the teacher cares and strengthens the consequence's impact.
Letting go of grudges once time-out ends, and keeping the classroom itself engaging, both reinforce why the consequence works.
quotes: Your classroom management plan doesn’t have to be complex to be effective. Four rules and three consequences will usually do the trick. Indeed, there is no magic in the plan itself.
Time-out is an excellent example. Undoubtedly the most commonly used consequence, time-out can be incredibly effective or a waste of time depending on how it’s carried out.
Model your time-out procedure by playing the part of a misbehaving student. Show your students exactly what is expected of them if they’re sent to time-out.
Whenever you enforce a classroom rule that requires a time-out, it’s important to tell the student why he or she is being separated from the rest of the class. Be brief and to the point.
Time-out doesn’t work well unless you’re supervising your students yourself. I realize this can be tough to do during a recess time-out . But it’s worth it.
After the time-out is over, it’s over. The student has paid the fine and is therefore a class member in good standing. Holding grudges and taking behavior personally will result in more bad behavior.

For time-out to be effective, your students must feel like they’re missing something. If your classroom is an exciting and interesting place to be, they will always feel like they’re missing something.
